beats.narration_text: There's a new AI model everyone is talking about this month. It's called Jev, and it comes from a startup called TypeSafe. This is Sai. If you've used a chatbot but never met Jev, this is the gentle version: what it is, what it's good for, and what it can't do.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hello, Sai'
three plain result lines land
'it doesn't write text' lands last and holds

props.segment: The Model That Doesn't Write Back
props.command: Everyone is talking about Jev. I've used ChatGPT, but I've never heard of TypeSafe. Explain Jev to me gently: what it does, what it doesn't do, and why developers are excited.
props.runningText: reading the launch post and the docs…
output: Jev · TypeSafe AI · early access since Sept 15
fast, cheap — and it doesn't write text

beats.narration_text: Start with an old job. A switchboard operator never wrote anyone a letter. A call came in, and in a moment they decided which line it belonged on. Jev is built for exactly that kind of quick decision. TypeSafe calls it a System One model, after the fast, intuitive System 1 in Daniel Kahneman's book, Thinking, Fast and Slow.

beats.narration_text: Here's the difference from a chatbot. Ask a chatbot something and it writes a reply, one word at a time, and then your program has to read that text to dig out the answer. Jev never writes. You hand it the situation and your questions, and every answer comes back at once, as a value your code can use directly.

it splits by who answers
the badges land: a typed answer, a paragraph

data.slideMeta: SAME QUESTION · TWO KINDS OF MODEL

beats.narration_text: Jev understands three kinds of question. A Choice: which of your options fits, like a sorting machine picking a bin. A Score: where on your scale, like a needle on a dial. And a yes-or-no that TypeSafe calls a Noul: is this true? Their own example asks three at once about a refund: was one requested, is it a duplicate, does policy allow it.

beats.narration_text: So what does that number mean? Jev's probabilities are meant to be calibrated. Take every answer it gave at 0.8, and about eight in ten should turn out true. In a simulation of a hundred answers at 0.8, eighty-two came out true. That's what 'about' means. And TypeSafe says it plainly: calibration doesn't promise any single answer is right.

props.title: When Jev says 0.8, what does it mean?
props.note: Calibrated: of all the answers given 0.8, about eight in ten turn out true.
props.conditions: s: a statement; p̂: Jev's probability that s is true. Calibration is measured across groups of predictions, not one answer (TypeSafe docs). Seeded check: 100 draws at 0.8 → 82 true (evidence/calibration.py).

beats.narration_text: Why are developers excited? Speed and price. TypeSafe says a reply takes seventy to five hundred milliseconds, and reading costs four point two cents per million tokens, with the answers free. Do the arithmetic: a million support tickets, at five hundred tokens each, comes to about twenty-one dollars. Those are TypeSafe's own numbers, though. Hold that thought.

show.event: the fastest and slowest reply times land
the price per million input tokens lands
the million-ticket total closes the table

props.title: What TypeSafe says it costs
props.note: TypeSafe's published figures (launch post, 15 Sep 2026); output is free. Last row: 1,000,000 tickets at an assumed 500 tokens each — arithmetic in evidence/cost.py.

beats.narration_text: TypeSafe also publishes a list of what Jev is bad at, which is refreshing. It isn't a calculator, so do your math in code. It reads dates as text, not as dates. Instructions hidden inside the input can steer it. And it doesn't write text at all. For now it only reads text, too: no images yet.

beats.narration_text: Which brings us to the fair question. The biggest claims, up to two hundred times faster, come from tests TypeSafe's own team built, and they say so. Nobody independent has verified them yet. The good news: Jev is cheap enough to test on your own work for pocket change. And 'can't hallucinate' means the answer always has the right shape, not that it's right.

beats.narration_text: So, gently: Jev is a model that answers instead of writing. Three kinds of question, answered at once, each with a number for how sure it is. Fast and cheap, by its maker's measure. Test it on your own work before you believe it.

the limits line closes it

props.artifactTitle: The Model That Doesn't Write Back
artifactLines: Jev is TypeSafe AI's first System One model, in early access since 15 September 2026. It answers questions from software with typed values and probabilities, never with text.
It knows three kinds of question — Choice, Score and Noul (yes or no) — and answers every question in a request together, in one pass.
TypeSafe says replies take 70–500 ms and input costs $0.042 per million tokens, output free. Its biggest speed and cost multiples come from its own tests.
It is not a calculator, reads dates as text, can be steered by hidden instructions and reads only text. The shape of each answer is guaranteed; its truth is yours to test.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick one decision your code makes today, maybe an if-statement, maybe a chatbot call. Ask an assistant to split it into Jev-sized questions: a yes-or-no, a choice, a score. Ask which parts should stay as plain code. And ask how you'd check that its eight in ten really means eight in ten, on your own data.
